1080: Send envoys to Hiraizumi and ask Hidehira to lead the men of Ōshū south
1082: Hold the Home Provinces and wait for Kamakura to tear itself apart
1085: One by one, the warriors of the Home Provinces slipped away. Kamakura's envoys promised to confirm their ancestral lands, and they quietly went home.
1086: The warrior monks said the mountain temples take no part in the quarrels of warrior houses.
1087: On a morning of spring rain, Yoshitsune came to take his leave. “Kurō will never forget the Cloistered Emperor's kindness as long as he lives,” he said. Then, with Benkei and Shizuka, he vanished into the rain.
1092: The In-zen, hidden in a mountain ascetic's pack, travelled for a month before it reached Hiraizumi.
1093: Hidehira read it in the Golden Hall of Chūson-ji. Within the hall, the remains of his father and grandfather—Kiyohira and Motohira—lay at rest beneath the Sumeru altar.
1094: “The Cloistered Emperor has entrusted the two provinces of Mutsu and Dewa to our Fujiwara house and to Kurō Hōgan. After I am dead, you shall serve Kurō as your commander-in-chief and uphold the In-zen against Kamakura. Whoever disobeys is no son of mine.”
1095: In the tenth month, Hidehira died. This time, with the In-zen in his hands, Yasuhira was no longer afraid.
1096: In Bunji 5, Yoritomo marched north with two hundred and eighty thousand horsemen. At Atsukashiyama he met one hundred and seventy thousand riders of Ōshū, commanded by Yoshitsune himself.
1099: The men of Ōshū were fierce, but Kamakura had more. The double moat at Atsukashiyama was breached, and Yoshitsune fell back to Koromogawa.
1100: Benkei stood before the residence, pierced by ten thousand arrows, and did not fall. Yoshitsune took his own life. Yasuhira was killed by his own retainers as he fled.
1101: In the ruins of Hiraizumi, Yoritomo found your In-zen. He made no noise about it. He simply had it carried back to the capital and laid upon your desk.
1102: Not a word came with it.
1104: You turned your In-zen back and forth among the Taira, the Minamoto, Kiso and the Hōgan, and died peacefully at sixty-six. Kamakura founded its shogunate.
1106: Four months after your death, in the 7th month of Kenkyū 3, Minamoto no Yoritomo was named *Sei-i Taishōgun*. From then on the Kamakura shogunate was the true master of Japan, for nearly a hundred and fifty years; after it came Muromachi and Edo, and the age of the warrior houses stretched on for almost seven hundred years.
1107: You left behind the thousand Kannon of Rengeō-in, the more than one hundred and eighty estates of the Chōkōdō domain, and the twenty scrolls of the Ryōjin Hishō—of which only a handful survive today. You left behind Emperor Go-Toba, the child who once clambered onto your knee. Twenty-nine years later he would raise an army against Kamakura in your manner, be defeated, and be exiled to Oki, never to see the capital again.
1108: Kujō Kanezane cursed you in his diary even as he recorded your every move. In the Gukanshō, Jien wrote that you had made the realm into 「武者の世」—the age of warriors. Yoritomo called you the Great Tengu. Yet even he admitted that without you, he would have remained forever an exile in Izu.
1109: You never held an army truly your own. You had only your In-zen, your imayō, and a patience that outlived everyone.
1110: 遊びをせんとや生まれけむ　戯れせんとや生まれけん
1111: The Cloistered Emperor Go-Shirakawa died on the 13th day of the 3rd month of Kenkyū 3 (1192), aged sixty-six. In the 7th month of that year, Minamoto no Yoritomo was appointed Sei-i Taishōgun. Most of the Ryōjin Hishō he compiled was lost; surviving fragments were discovered only at the end of the Meiji era.
1114: The In's decrees and the In's own troops stood side by side, and the warrior houses became the sovereign's vassals at last. The Emperor ruled the realm in person.
1115: Authority and Arms both strong, with an Emperor worthy of the succession.
1116: As you lay dying, you summoned Emperor Go-Toba to your bedside. He was thirteen, his eyes as bright as the year he first climbed onto your knee.
1117: “Cloistered rule ends with me. From this day on, the Emperor governs the realm himself.”
1118: The Northern and Western Guards you had gathered over the years, the warrior monks of Enryaku-ji and Kōfuku-ji, the wealth of the Chōkōdō and Rengeō-in estates—all of it passed into his hands. The warrior houses of Kamakura were constables in name and the sovereign's vassals in fact; Yoritomo was made Major Captain of the Right Palace Guards, and still had to come up to the capital each year to pay homage.
1119: Once Go-Toba took the reins, he rebuilt the Daigokuden—the great hall that had burned in the Angen fire and was never meant to rise again. On the day of his enthronement he sat upon the Takamikura and watched the courtiers and the warriors of the eastern provinces prostrate themselves below as one.
1120: Later histories would call this age the “Kenkyū Restoration.” The golden reigns of Engi and Tenryaku, returned after three hundred years.
1121: Only no one knew how many generations such a realm could last. The warriors had already tasted power.
1122: Historically, in Jōkyū 3 (1221), the Retired Emperor Go-Toba raised troops against the Kamakura regent Hōjō Yoshitoki, was defeated, and was exiled to Oki—the Jōkyū Disturbance. Thereafter the court had no power to stand against the shogunate until the Kenmu Restoration.
1123: A Thousand Years of Cloistered Rule
1125: Minamoto and Taira stood apart, and the In sat between them. The realm was a balance scale, and you were its fulcrum.
1126: With a cunning heart, keep the warrior houses forever in check against one another.
1127: After your death, the warriors of east and west still glared at each other across Hakone and Suzuka. Neither dared move first—for whichever moved first would at once receive an In-zen calling for its destruction.
1128: Your heirs learned your art: promotions for the east today, lands for the west tomorrow; letters of comfort in one hand, secret orders to arm in the other. The In-zen hung like a blade forever suspended, never truly falling.
1129: Later historians were torn over this age. Some called it the most peaceful era Japan ever knew—four hundred years without a great war. Others called it the most rotten—a court held together by sowing discord rather than by virtuous rule, while hatred among the warriors piled up layer upon layer, never to be dissolved.
1130: Each year in the 3rd month, on the old grounds of Hōjūji-dono, people still sing imayō. The Cloistered Emperor of the day sits behind the blinds, softly keeping time.
1131: It is no longer you. But it looks very much like you.
1132: Historically, in his last years Go-Shirakawa strove to keep a balance between the In and the warrior houses, but after the Ōshū campaign and Yoritomo's visit to the capital, Kamakura's advantage was unshakable. Cloistered rule survived in form into the Edo period, but its real power was essentially lost after the Jōkyū Disturbance.
1135: Rokuhara never fell, and the red banners flew forever. Emperor Antoku grew to manhood, and the age of the Heike went on.
1136: Share Kiyomori's boat and hold off the east together.
1137: Within a few years the eastern rebellions were put down. Yoritomo died in Sagami, Yoshinaka in the Hokuriku, and Hidehira of Ōshū sent envoys with gifts of horses in token of submission.
1138: Emperor Antoku grew up a gentle, studious sovereign. His mother Tokuko was empress dowager; his uncles Munemori, Tomomori and Shigehira sat among the high nobles. Sixteen Taira kugyō, more than thirty courtiers of the privy chamber, more than thirty provinces held in proprietorship—and Tokitada's saying, “Whoever is not of the Heike is not human,” still went around the capital.
1139: You lived out your old age in peace at Hōjūji-dono. The Heike treated you with the utmost deference and did everything in the name of your In-zen—though whose hand actually wrote those decrees, everyone understood without saying.
1140: Fukuhara became a second capital, and Song ships came and went endlessly at Ōwada-no-tomari. Song coins flowed through every province, and the capital saw its first townsmen buying rice with money. Some said that if the age went on like this, Japan would become a merchant nation of the sea.
1141: 祇園精舎の鐘の声, the echo of the impermanence of all things—that book was never written.
1142: Historically, the Heike fled the capital in Juei 2 (1183) and were destroyed at Dan-no-ura in Genryaku 2 (1185). The saying “Whoever is not of the Heike is not human” is traditionally attributed to Taira no Tokitada; see The Tale of the Heike, Book One.
1144: Kyoto and Yashima, each serving its own emperor. The Cloistered Emperor died in a temporary palace on the western sea, and the realm was split in two.
1145: Go west with the Heike and hold fast without giving battle.
1146: You spent the rest of your life in the temporary palace at Yashima. The sea wind was strong, and the blinds were forever slapping in it.
1147: Emperor Go-Toba in Kyoto and Emperor Antoku at Yashima, the Inland Sea between them, each issued his own edicts, each appointed his own governors, each called the other a false emperor. Yoritomo in the east served Kyoto; Kyūshū and Shikoku served Yashima. The Inland Sea became a border.
1148: After your death, the Heike built you a small imperial tomb at Yashima, facing east—facing Kyoto.
1149: This division between two emperors lasted more than sixty years. Later generations called it Japan's “first Northern and Southern Courts”—though in truth they were Eastern and Western.
1150: The sacred regalia in the west, the Emperor in the east. Which side was legitimate? Centuries later, people were still arguing.
1151: Historically, Go-Shirakawa slipped away to Mount Hiei and did not go west with the Heike. But a split between two imperial lines did come to pass, between 1336 and 1392, in the era of the Northern and Southern Courts.
1153: You followed the Heike all the way west, and at last sank to the bottom of the sea with Emperor Antoku at Dan-no-ura.
1154: Go west with the Heike, when the Heike cannot hold.
1155: Ichi-no-Tani was lost. Yashima was lost. The Heike fleet fell back westward, all the way to Dan-no-ura in Nagato Province.
1156: On the afternoon of the 24th day of the 3rd month, the tide turned. Seated in the imperial vessel, you watched the red banners go down one after another.
1157: The Nun of the Second Rank lifted Emperor Antoku in her arms and went to the gunwale. She looked back at you once.
1158: “Come, Your Holiness, you too. 浪の下にも都のさぶらふぞ。 (There is a capital beneath the waves as well.)”
1159: You rose to your feet. Your fifty-nine-year-old body was lighter than you had imagined.
1160: The water was cold, and then it was not cold. The last thing you heard was the shouting of Minamoto warriors on the surface—they were crying “Your Holiness! Your Holiness!”—but the voices grew farther and farther away, as if heard through a very heavy blind.
1161: Later, the fishermen of Shimonoseki said that the crabs of Dan-no-ura bore samurai faces on their backs. They called them *Heike crabs*.
1162: Historically, Emperor Antoku and Tokiko, the Nun of the Second Rank, threw themselves into the sea at Dan-no-ura; he was eight years old. Go-Shirakawa remained in the capital. The legend of the Heike crab is told around Shimonoseki.
1164: You gave the sword of command to the fierce general of Kiso. He held the Uji River, and he held you.
1165: Trust Yoshinaka, and give him enough troops.
1166: In the battle of the Uji River, Yoshinaka, outnumbered, drove back the eastern army with the help of a flank attack by the warrior monks of Mount Hiei. Yoshitsune was wounded in the melee, and Noriyori fell back to Ōmi.
1167: Yoritomo did not come again. He fell ill in Kamakura and died three years later, and the great houses of the east turned on one another.
1168: Yoshinaka became the guardian of the capital. He never understood waka, never lost his Kiso accent, and made himself a laughingstock at court countless times. But he was utterly loyal to you, and when you died he knelt outside Rokujō-dono for three days and three nights.
1169: Tomoe Gozen later became a warrior of the In's Northern Guard—said to be the first woman warrior in Japan ever granted an official post.
1170: Yoshinaka died ten years after you, in his forties. His grave is at Awazu in Ōmi—those frozen paddies. He went back to them in the end, only twenty years late.
1171: Historically, Yoshinaka was killed in battle at Awazu in Ōmi on the 20th day of the 1st month of Juei 3 (1184), aged thirty-one. His grave is at Gichū-ji in present-day Ōtsu, Shiga Prefecture; by his own last wish, Matsuo Bashō was buried beside it.
1172: With the In's decrees and the In's troops behind him, Kurō Hōgan drove Kamakura back. The quarrel of brothers ended with the younger victorious.
1173: After the night attack at Horikawa, give Yoshitsune a real army.
1174: Three times Kamakura's armies marched west, and three times they were thrown back in Ōmi and Mino. Yoshitsune commanded like a god, and with Hidehira of Ōshū pressing from the north, Kamakura was beset front and rear.
1175: In Bunji 5, Hōjō Tokimasa and Hiki Yoshikazu came to blows, and Kamakura fell into civil strife. After a fall from his horse, Yoritomo took to his bed and sent men to the capital to sue for peace.
1176: You named Yoshitsune *Sei-i Taishōgun*. He was the first warrior chieftain to found a shogunate in the capital—its seat at Rokujō-Horikawa, right beside your palace.
1177: “All my life, and at last someone is willing to tell Kurō, ‘You did well.’”
1178: Yet you knew, too, that the Hōgan was the finest general in the realm, but not necessarily a good ruler. He did not understand Yoritomo's methods—vassals, confirmation of ancestral lands, the apportioning of rewards. After your death, his shogunate lasted only a single generation.
1179: And yet it is always he whom people remember. A thousand years on, the word 「判官びいき」—a soft spot for the fallen hero—is still current in Japan.
1180: Historically, Yoshitsune took his own life at the Koromogawa residence on the 30th day of the intercalary 4th month of Bunji 5 (1189), aged thirty-one. The word 「判官びいき」 comes from him.
1181: One hundred and seventy thousand horsemen of Ōshū drove back Yoritomo at Atsukashiyama. From then on, Japan was divided in three.
1182: Send a secret In-zen to Hidehira, having already become a tengu.
1183: Below the double moat at Atsukashiyama, the great army of Kamakura bogged down in the autumn rain. Yoshitsune burst out from a ridge on the flank, and Yoritomo's center broke.
1184: Yoritomo withdrew to Kamakura and never again dared look north.
1185: The Ōshū Fujiwara endured at Hiraizumi. The golden halls and pagodas of Chūson-ji and Mōtsū-ji grew ever more splendid, and gold dust from the Kitakami River flowed unceasingly to the capital—to the In. Mutsu became a half-independent kingdom, following the capital's calendar but governing itself.
1186: After your death, Japan had three centers: the In in Kyoto, the warrior house in Kamakura, the Fujiwara in Hiraizumi. Each held the others in check, and none could swallow the rest.
1187: Later people said it was the last and greatest game of sugoroku of your life. The dice fell exactly where you wanted them.
1188: Historically, the Ōshū campaign (1189) ended with the defeat and death of Fujiwara no Yasuhira, and the Ōshū Fujiwara perished after four generations and a hundred years. The Golden Hall of Chūson-ji still stands today.
1190: You entrusted the court to Kujō Kanezane. The Fujiwara house of regents rose again after you were gone.
1191: Entrust the government to Kanezane, and treat the house of regents generously.
1192: After your death, Kujō Kanezane became the true master of the court. The man who had cursed you in his diary all his life inherited your realm in the end.
1193: He set court ceremonial in order and revived many of the old rites that had fallen into neglect in your day. Yoritomo respected him, and between Kamakura and the capital there was a rare season of harmony.
1194: Kanezane's younger brother Jien became head of the Tendai school and wrote a book called the Gukanshō. In it he said that the history of Japan has its own “principle,” and that the regents and the warrior houses together assisting the Emperor was the principle of this age.
1195: But “principle” sometimes changes. In Kanezane's later years, Minamoto no Michichika joined with Lady Tango to stage a coup and drove him from the court. He took the tonsure and withdrew, and in the last pages of his diary he began to write of you again.
1196: “If only the Cloistered Emperor were still here…” He wrote that much, and laid down his brush.
1197: Kujō Kanezane became regent in Bunji 2 (1186) and fell from power in Kenkyū 7 (1196) in Minamoto no Michichika's coup, known as the “Coup of Kenkyū 7.” His diary, the Gyokuyō, is the most important source for the study of this period.
1200: You never held the realm tight. All you held was the rhythm of a song.
1201: Bring the way of imayō to perfection, and do not cling to power.
1202: At last you laid down the In-zen.
1203: In your later years you scarcely concerned yourself with government at all. Kamakura, the regents, the Emperor—let them do as they would. At Rokujō-dono you gathered the puppeteer women, shirabyōshi dancers and courtesans of the realm, sang with them, revised the Ryōjin Hishō with them, and wrote down every old melody you had learned from Otomae.
1204: Some said you had grown senile. Others said you were guarding this country in another way—guarding the voices that would never be written into the histories: the sighs of courtesans, the prayers of farmers, the play-songs of children, the nembutsu on the Kumano road.
1205: As you lay dying, you had Lady Tango help you sit up, and sang one last song. Your voice was very soft, as it had been when you were a boy.
1206: 遊びをせんとや生まれけむ　戯れせんとや生まれけん　遊ぶ子供の声聞けば　我が身さへこそ揺るがるれ
1207: —Were we born to play? Were we born to frolic? When I hear the voices of children at play, even this body of mine begins to sway.
1208: The Ryōjin Hishō originally consisted of ten scrolls of lyrics and ten scrolls of the Kudenshū. Today only a fragment of lyrics scroll one and scroll two survive, along with a fragment of Kudenshū scroll one and scroll ten. Scroll two was not discovered until Meiji 44 (1911).
1211: You refused your brother's sutras written in blood, and lost the hearts of the temples as well. As you lay dying, the tengu of Shiramine came for you.
1212: Reject Sutoku's sutras, lose the Temples, and let the Tengu run deep.
1213: On the nights when you lay gravely ill, someone at Rokujō-dono always heard the beating of wings.
1214: The physicians said it was the wind. The yin-yang masters said it was a vengeful spirit. Lady Tango chanted the nembutsu at your bedside all night long. But you knew who it was.
1215: He stood outside the blinds, his hair and nails grown impossibly long, his robes in tatters, a pair of black wings sprouting from his back. He simply stood there, neither coming in nor going away.
1216: “Masahito, do you still remember the cherry blossoms at Hōkongō-in?”
1217: You wanted to answer, but no sound would come.
1218: In later legend, Retired Emperor Sutoku became one of the three great vengeful spirits of Japan, ranked alongside Sugawara no Michizane and Taira no Masakado. People said every upheaval since Hōgen—Heiji, Jishō, Juei, Jōkyū—was his curse. Seven hundred years later, before his enthronement, Emperor Meiji sent envoys to the Shiramine tomb in Sanuki to bring Sutoku's spirit back to the capital, and built the Shiramine Shrine to worship it.
1219: By then you had been dead for six hundred and seventy-six years.
1220: Belief in Sutoku's vengeful spirit arose in the Angen era. In Keiō 4 (1868), Emperor Meiji sent envoys to bring Sutoku's spirit back to the capital and built the Shiramine Shrine.
1223: You gave up the throne, and spent your whole life singing imayō in the courtesans' inns along the Yodo River.
1225: You did not accept the crown.
1226: Bifukumon-in was furious; Shinzei shook his head and sighed. In the end Morihito ascended the throne directly, with the Retired Emperor Toba himself assisting in government. You were stripped of a prince's privileges and moved out of the capital.
1227: You went to Eguchi, where the Yodo and Kanzaki rivers meet, and where the courtesans rowed their little boats beneath the moon, singing to passing travellers. You lived with them, sang with them, drank with them.
1228: Later, many things happened in the capital. The Hōgen Disturbance, the Heiji Disturbance, the rise and fall of the Heike, the rise of the Genji—you heard of it all only from merchants passing through.
1229: One autumn, a monk passing through Eguchi took shelter from the rain under a courtesan's eaves. He heard someone inside singing imayō, and singing it superbly. He asked, “Who is singing?”
1231: The courtesan laughed. “An old gentleman. He says he used to be the Emperor.”
1232: The monk took it for a jest, laughed, and went on his way. His name was Saigyō.
1233: Historically, Go-Shirakawa took the throne in Kyūju 2 (1155). The exchange of waka between Saigyō and Tae, a courtesan of Eguchi, appears in the Sankashū and the Shin Kokin Wakashū, and was later adapted into the Noh play Eguchi.
